Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Kwakye Ofosu challenges NPP’s principle on presidential jet purchase, cites 2000 parliamentary debate Source : Emma Ankrah 17 November 2026 5:48pm Minister of State in charge of Government Communications, Felix Kwakye Ofosu ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Government Spokesperson Felix Kwakye Ofosu has questioned the New Patriotic Party's (NPP) consistency on presidential aircraft purchases, citing the party's opposition to the acquisition of an aircraft by the Jerry Rawlings administration in 2000.
He says the party cannot accuse the current government of abandoning its principles over the purchase of a new presidential jet without accounting for its own position when it was in opposition.
Speaking on JoyNews' The Pulse on Tuesday, November 17, Mr Kwakye Ofosu challenged the Ranking Member on Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, to explain what he described as the NPP's inconsistent position on the matter.
Reading from the February 15, 2000 edition of the Parliamentary Hansard, Mr Kwakye Ofosu quoted Nana Akufo-Addo as saying that at a time when the country needed greater public investment in health and tertiary education, the government was considering spending $19 million over five years on an aircraft for the President.
“When he [Samuel Abu Jinapor] speaks about principle, I also can challenge this principle. Where was his principle? Where was the NPP's principle? Where was President Akufo-Addo's principle? In the year 2000, they stood in Parliament and the parliamentary Hansard captures it, and attacked the Rawlings administration for buying an aircraft when they came to power. In fact, they ordered two aircraft. It was President Mills who cancelled one. Otherwise, we would have had two aircraft,” he said.
His comments follow criticism by Samuel Abu Jinapor, who challenged the government's position on presidential aircraft purchases, arguing that its current decision contradicts its earlier criticism of the Akufo-Addo administration.
The Government Spokesperson accused the NPP of selectively invoking the principle of consistency in the current debate while overlooking its own past positions.
He argued that the party was demanding accountability over the current government's aircraft purchase but did not want its historical position on presidential aircraft acquisitions brought into the discussion.
On the criticism of former President Akufo-Addo's use of expensive chartered aircraft, Mr Kwakye Ofosu said he stood by his comments and saw no reason to apologise.
“Absolutely not. People speak about an apology. Look, there is no apology to be had. Apologise for what? Calling out a president who chose to waste our money,” he said.
He maintained that the criticism was justified because of the economic conditions Ghana was experiencing under the previous administration.
“At a time when the president plunged all of us into hardship, he decided that he needed to live like an Arabian king,” he said.
Mr Kwakye Ofosu argued that the criticism was not about denying the President the right to travel safely but about the cost of the arrangements made for his official trips.
He said the previous administration could have opted for more affordable aircraft or commercial flights when the presidential jet was unavailable, rather than incur the cost of expensive chartered flights.
